Reasons for Land Revolts in India
Before Independence, there were three major land reforms prevailing in the country:
1. Permanent Settlement Lord Cornwallis introduced Daroga System replacing 2. Ryotwari System Zamindari Thanedars.
3. Mahalwari System
Permanent Settlement (1793)
Introduced by: Lord Cornwallis.
Planned by: John Shore.

Tribal Revolts in India during British Rules Bhil Sewaram Kazi Singh 1818 Khandesh, Revolt (Khajya Naik), Bhima Maharashtra Naik Ho Revolt · Raja Parahat 1820-1821 · Singhbhum,. Jharkhand + It is also known as "Zamindari System".
Under the Zamindari system, the land revenue was collected from the farmers by the intermediaries known as Zamindars (the middle man).
It was introduced in: Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh.

A sunset clause was introduced in the Zamindari system that required zamindars to pay afixed amount of revenue by a specific date, before sunset. If the zamindars failed to pay the revenue on time, the government would confiscate and auction off their zamindari, which was hereditary.
Ryotwari System (1820)
Introduced by: Thomas Munro and Captain Alexander Read.
It was based on Ricardian Theory of Rent.
Under the Ryotwari system (Ryot: Peasant), the land revenue was paid by the farmers directly to the state.
It was introduced in: South India (Madras region of Tamil Nadu).
Mahalwari System (1822)
Introduced by: Holt Mackenzie (Concept) and later reformed by William Bentinck (1833).
It was introduced in: North-Western Provinces, Central India, Punjab, and parts of Uttar Pradesh (Gangetic Valley).
Under the Mahalwari system, the land revenue was collected from the farmers by the village headmen on behalf of the whole village (and not the zamindar).
The village or group of villages was termed a "Mahal" and treated as a single revenue unit.

Reasons for Failure of 1857 Revolt
Due to limited territorial and social base, the revolt was primarily concentrated in North India.
Lack of coordination and leadership.
Lack of political perspective.
VD Savarkarstated it as "First war of Independence".
RC Majumdar: It is neither "First'', nor "National" nor a "War of Independence".
Government of India Act 1858
East India Company was abolished.
Queen's Proclamation— Crown Rule (transfer of power from East India Company to the British Crown). Queen Victoria was the then Queen.
The British significantly restructured the Indian Army, and the proportion of Indian soldiers was reduced (on the recommendation of the Peel Commission).
Governor-General became Viceroy > 1st Viceroy: Lord Canning.
Indigo Revolt (1859)
It started in Nadia (District) of Bengal.
Leaders: Digambar Biswas and Bishnucharan Biswas.
It was against the exploitative practices of British planters who forced Indian farmers to cultivate indigo instead of food crops on their land.
It was a successful revolt.
Dinbandhu Mitrawrote "Nil Darpan' (a play about Indigo Revolt). The play was translated into English by the famous Bengali poet and playwright Michael Madhusudan Dutt.

The Hindoo Patriot, an English weekly started in 1853 at Calcutta by Girish Chandra Ghosh and later edited by Harish Chandra Mukherjee, exposed the atrocities of British indigo planters and supported peasants during the Indigo Revolt.
Deccan Revolt (1875)
Itstarted in Maharashtra (Deccan region).
+ Cause: Agrarian riots against moneylenders and debt bonds.
Background: The Cotton Boom
Before 1861, Britain imported 3/4th of its cotton from America.
American Civil War (1861): Supply from America stopped. Britain turned to India.
Cotton Supply Association (1857): Formed in Britain to encourage Indian farmers to grow cotton for British industries. Farmers took loans to expand cultivation, expecting high profits.
However, after the end of the American Civil War, the demand for Indian cotton declined sharply, leading to losses for farmers.
Manchester Cotton Company was formed in 1859 Result:
